definition: Wind generation output depends heavily on the exact physical location of a turbine, not just the general region — nearby sites can have very different wind resource quality.
core_idea: Terrain features (e.g., a hilltop versus the sheltered side of the same hill) can produce sharply different wind speeds at locations only a short distance apart, so wind resource assessment must be done at the individual turbine/site level rather than assumed uniform across a project area.
key_points: Two nearby locations can have materially different wind conditions due to terrain (e.g., hilltop vs. hillside shelter).
This makes wind output forecasting and siting more granular/site-specific than for some other generation types.
relationships: Affects capacity factor estimates used in wind project economics
trading_implications: Forecast error for a specific wind farm can't be assumed to track a regional average; site-level historical output data is more reliable than nearby-site proxies.
caveats: Assuming that wind conditions are roughly uniform across a small geographic area.
